newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST-Analysts divided on Italy rate cut timing.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Analysts divided on Italy rate cut timing.

text.p: Economists are largely divided over whether the Bank of Italy will cut interest rates this week after preliminary April CPI figures or wait a little longer due to worries over the lira and uncertainty over Italy's EMU entry.

A Reuters survey on Tuesday showed a mixed picture over when the Bank will cut rates -- either this week or later -- with the outlook clouded given a lira weaker than its 990 lire/mark ERM central parity and uncertainty over Italy's early entry to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Analysts forecast a rate cut of 50 to 75 basis points.

Preliminary data from six Italian cities on Monday pointed to April consumer price inflation of 1.8 percent, down from March's 2.2 percent. The final five cities report at 1530 GMT Tuesday and some say CPI may even fall to 1.7 percent.
The lira on Tuesday slipped to 998.85 against the mark due to the dollar's slide and the weakness of the French franc. At 1335 GMT the lira was quoted at 997.70/7.95 per mark.

"With CPI under 1.8 percent, the Bank of Italy has to cut," said Martino Dofini at Chase. "With a cut the lira would appreciate and this would be a signal that the central bank is confident that things are going well," he added.

Sharda Persaud of San Paolo Bank saw a cut later Tuesday of 50 basis points. "The market is already discounting a cut in rates by the end of the year and a cut of 50 basis points is quite small and will not be a risk for the lira," she added.

"The current weakness of the lira is more linked to international factors and is of a temporary nature. I do not believe that this is sufficient to prevent a cut in rates," said Lorenzo Codogno of Bank of America.
But for other analysts, the Bank of Italy must delay a cut until the lira returns to near its 990 parity and until there is less turbulence in financial markets.
Davide Tesoro of Indosuez saw a cut by the end of May with a return of lira/mark to under 990. "The Bank of Italy must hold to this objective," he added.

For Gianluca Sanna of Stone & McCarthy, there are two obstacles to a cut by the end of the week. "First, I believe that the Bank of Italy wants to see the reaction of the market to the provisional EU report and then assess the lira. At this level of exchange it is dangerous to cut rates," he added.

On Wednesday, the EU Commission will release a report on member's economies and press reports have said it will show Italy above the three percent deficit/GDP ratio for 1997 needed for single currency entry in January, 1999.
For Pio De Gregorio at NatWest, despite the sharp fall in inflation markets remain too turbulent, uncertain both on the international and on the domestic side.

On the overseas front De Gregorio cited the up-coming snap elections in France. Within Italy, the mini-budget must be approved soon, and the presentation of the government's three-year economic plan (DPEF) is due by mid-May.
"The DPEF will have an enormous political importance for the progress of our relationship with our European partners and also for the budget for 1998," said De Gregorio.
The majority of analysts noted that this will not necessarily be the last interest rate cut by the central bank.
The Bank of Italy has cut its discount rate three times in the last 10 months, each time by 75 basis points, to the current 6.75 percent.
The following are the results of the survey.
When do you see an interest rate cut?
By the end of the week (6 out of 11)
By the end of the month (1/11)
By the end of May (3/11)
During June (1/11)
How much will the cut be?
50 basis points (7/11)
75 basis points (4/11)

Note - the following banks took part in the survey: Banque Indosuez, Bank of America, Natwest, Cariplo, Credito Italiano, CSFB, Deutsche Bank, San Paolo Bank, Stone & McCarthy, Nomura and Chase Manhattan Bank.
